{{short description|On constructing an aspherical CW complex whose fundamental group is a given group}}
In [[mathematics]], particularly in [[homological algebra]] and [[algebraic topology]], the '''Eilenberg–Ganea theorem''' states for every finitely generated group ''G'' with certain conditions on its [[cohomological dimension]] (namely <math>3\le \operatorname{cd}(G)\le n</math>), one can construct an [[aspherical space|aspherical]] [[CW complex]] ''X'' of dimension ''n'' whose [[fundamental group]] is&nbsp;''G''. The theorem is named after Polish mathematician [[Samuel Eilenberg]] and Romanian mathematician [[Tudor Ganea]]. The theorem was first published in a short paper in 1957 in the ''[[Annals of Mathematics]]''.<ref>**{{Cite journal |first1=Samuel |last1=Eilenberg |authorlink1=Samuel Eilenberg|first2=Tudor |last2=Ganea |authorlink2=Tudor Ganea| title=On the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category of abstract groups |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |series=2nd Ser. |volume=65 |year=1957 |issue=3 |pages=517–518 |doi=10.2307/1970062 |jstor=1970062 |mr=0085510 }}</ref>

==Definitions==
'''Group cohomology:''' Let <math>G</math> be a group and let <math>X=K(G,1)</math> be the corresponding [[Eilenberg−MacLane space]]. Then we have the following singular [[chain complex]] which is a [[Resolution (algebra)|free resolution]] of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> over the [[group ring]] <math>\mathbb{Z}[G]</math> (where <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> is a trivial <math>\mathbb{Z}[G]</math>-module):

:<math>\cdots \xrightarrow{\delta_n+1} C_n(E)\xrightarrow{\delta_n} C_{n-1}(E)\rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow C_1(E)\xrightarrow{\delta_1} C_0(E)\xrightarrow{\varepsilon} \Z\rightarrow 0,</math>

where <math>E</math> is the universal cover of <math>X</math> and <math>C_k(E)</math> is the [[free abelian group]] generated by the singular <math>k</math>-chains on <math>E</math>.  The [[group cohomology]] of the group <math>G</math> with coefficient in a <math>\Z[G]</math>-module <math>M</math> is the cohomology of this [[chain complex]] with coefficients in <math>M</math>, and is denoted by <math>H^*(G,M)</math>.

'''Cohomological dimension:''' A group <math>G</math> has cohomological dimension <math>n</math> with coefficients in <math>\Z</math> (denoted by <math>\operatorname{cd}_{\Z}(G)</math>) if 
:<math>n=\sup \{k : \text{There exists a }\Z[G]\text{ module }M\text{ with }H^{k}(G,M)\neq 0\}. </math>

'''Fact:''' If <math>G</math> has a [[projective resolution]] of length at most <math>n</math>, i.e., <math>\Z</math> as trivial <math>\Z[G]</math> module has a projective resolution of length at most <math>n</math> if and only if <math>H^i_{\Z}(G,M)=0</math> for all <math>\Z</math>-modules <math>M</math> and for all <math>i>n</math>.{{citation needed|date=May 2012}}

Therefore, we have an alternative definition of cohomological dimension as follows,

''The cohomological dimension of G with coefficient in'' <math>\Z</math> ''is the smallest n (possibly infinity) such that G has a projective resolution of length'' ''n'', i.e., <math>\Z</math> ''has a projective resolution of length'' ''n'' ''as a trivial'' <math>\Z[G]</math> ''module.''

==Eilenberg−Ganea theorem==
Let <math>G</math> be a finitely presented group and <math>n\ge 3</math> be an integer. Suppose the [[cohomological dimension]] of <math>G</math> with coefficients in <math>\Z</math> is at most <math>n</math>, i.e., <math>\operatorname{cd}_{\Z}(G)\le n</math>.  Then there exists an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[aspherical space|aspherical]] [[CW complex]] <math>X</math> such that the [[fundamental group]] of <math>X</math> is <math>G</math>, i.e., <math>\pi_1(X)=G</math>.

==Converse==
Converse of this theorem is a consequence of [[cellular homology]], and the fact that every free module is projective.

'''Theorem:''' Let ''X'' be an aspherical ''n''-dimensional CW complex with ''π''<sub>1</sub>(''X'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''G'', then cd<sub>''Z''</sub>(''G'')&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''n''.

==Related results and conjectures==
For ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 the result is one of the consequences of [[Stallings theorem about ends of groups]].<ref>* [[John R. Stallings]], "On torsion-free groups with infinitely many ends", ''[[Annals of Mathematics]]'' '''88''' (1968), 312&ndash;334. {{MathSciNet|id=0228573}}</ref>

'''Theorem:''' Every finitely generated group of cohomological dimension one is free.

For <math>n=2</math> the statement is  known as the [[Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture]].

'''Eilenberg−Ganea Conjecture:''' If a group ''G'' has cohomological dimension 2 then there is a 2-dimensional aspherical CW complex ''X'' with <math>\pi_1(X)=G</math>.

It is known that given a group ''G'' with <math>\operatorname{cd}_{\Z}(G)=2</math>, there exists a 3-dimensional aspherical CW complex ''X'' with <math>\pi_1(X)=G</math>.
